description: The four factors of production — land, labour, capital and enterprise — and the reward each earns.
content_html:
What Are the Factors of Production?

Every good or service you can think of — from a can of Coca-Cola to a haircut to an Amazon delivery — is produced using resources. Economists group these resources into four categories called the factors of production. Understanding them is the starting point for understanding how any economy works, because production is impossible without combining all four.

Land

Land in economics means far more than fields and plots. It covers every natural resource used in production: the North Sea oil that powers heating systems, the iron ore smelted into steel, the timber felled for furniture, the fresh water used in food processing, even the electromagnetic spectrum used by mobile networks. Land has a fixed total supply — no one can manufacture more North Sea oilfields. This scarcity is why natural resources command a price. The reward paid to the owners of land is called rent.

Some natural resources are renewable — fish stocks can recover if harvested sustainably, forests can be replanted — while others, such as coal and crude oil, are non-renewable. Once extracted, they are gone permanently. This distinction matters for long-run production decisions and for questions of sustainability.

Labour

Labour is the physical and mental work people contribute to production. A nurse treating patients, a software developer writing code, a warehouse operative packing boxes, a teacher delivering a lesson — all are providing labour. The total supply of labour in an economy depends on the size of the working-age population, the proportion willing to work (the participation rate), and the number of hours worked. The reward for labour is wages (or salaries).

Labour is not uniform. A brain surgeon and a checkout operator both supply labour, but their productivity, skills and qualifications differ enormously — which is why their wages differ enormously too. Economists distinguish between skilled labour (requiring training, qualifications or experience) and unskilled labour. Investment in education and training raises the quality of labour, which is why governments spend heavily on schools and apprenticeship programmes.

Key Fact

The four factors of production and their rewards are: Land → Rent; Labour → Wages; Capital → Interest; Enterprise → Profit. These rewards are the incomes that flow to resource owners in return for their contribution to production.

Capital

Capital in economics does not mean money. It means man-made assets used to produce other goods and services. A factory floor, a delivery lorry, a 3D printer, a wind turbine, a computer server — these are all capital goods. The reward paid to the providers of capital (for instance, those who lend money to buy machinery) is interest.

Capital is crucial because it raises the productive capacity of labour. A bricklayer with a mechanical mixer lays far more bricks per hour than one mixing by hand. A farmer with a combine harvester processes far more grain than one using a scythe. Spending on capital goods is called investment, and it is one of the main drivers of long-run economic growth.

A common source of confusion is between capital goods and consumer goods. Capital goods are produced in order to make other things — a factory robot, a delivery van, a commercial oven in a bakery. Consumer goods are produced to satisfy final demand directly — a pizza, a pair of trainers, a smartphone. The same physical object can sometimes be either, depending on its use: a van bought by a plumber is a capital good; the same model of van bought by a family for holidays is a consumer good. The key question is: is this asset used to produce something else, or is it consumed directly?

Enterprise

Enterprise is the organising factor. The entrepreneur brings the other three factors together, takes decisions about what to produce and how to produce it, and bears the financial risk if things go wrong. When a school-leaver spends their savings setting up a food van at a local market — buying ingredients (land), employing a friend (labour), purchasing equipment (capital) — they are acting as an entrepreneur.

The reward for enterprise is profit — the income left over after all other costs have been paid. Profit is both a reward for risk-taking and an incentive that encourages new businesses to form and existing ones to innovate. If no profit is available, the incentive to combine the other factors of production disappears.

Key Fact

The entrepreneur is the factor that bears risk. They combine land, labour and capital in the hope of making a profit. Without the prospect of profit, there is no incentive to take on the risk of production — which is why profit motivates entrepreneurial activity in a market economy.

Factor Mobility

Factors of production are not always easy to move from one use to another. Factor mobility describes how freely a resource can shift to where it is most needed. There are two types: occupational mobility (moving between different jobs or industries) and geographical mobility (moving to a different location).

Occupational mobility is the ability to switch between industries or job types. A nurse who retrains as a physiotherapist is occupationally mobile; a coal miner who cannot retrain for a new industry is occupationally immobile. Low occupational mobility causes structural unemployment — workers are left behind when industries decline because their skills do not transfer easily.

Geographical mobility is the ability to move to a different location for work. A graduate who moves from Manchester to London for a new job is geographically mobile; a worker who cannot move because they own a home in a depressed region, or because family ties keep them in place, is geographically immobile. Both types of immobility create persistent regional inequalities in employment and wages — a major policy challenge for governments.

In general, land is the least mobile factor — a coal seam cannot be relocated. Capital can be more mobile (a vehicle or computer can be redeployed relatively easily, though a purpose-built factory is hard to convert). Labour varies in mobility depending on skills and personal circumstances. Enterprise is highly mobile in the sense that entrepreneurs can pivot from one business idea to another, though specialist expertise may limit this in practice.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘identify’ or ‘state’ a factor of production, just name it — land, labour, capital or enterprise. A common mistake is to confuse capital with money: in economics, capital means man-made equipment used in production, not cash. Another frequent error is writing ‘profit’ as the reward for capital — it is interest for capital, profit for enterprise. For ‘Explain’ questions, always add a chain: state the factor, describe what it is, give a real-world example, and connect it to the reward earned. For longer ‘Analyse’ or ‘Evaluate’ questions on factor mobility, model both sides — when mobility is high versus when it is low — and reach a judgement on which factor is hardest to move and why.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Every good and service is produced using a combination of four factors: land (natural resources → rent), labour (human effort → wages), capital (man-made equipment → interest) and enterprise (risk-bearing organisation → profit).
  • The entrepreneur is the key factor: they combine the other three, take on risk, and are rewarded with profit — the income remaining after all other costs are paid.
  • Factor mobility (occupational and geographical) determines how easily resources can shift to where they are most needed — immobility causes unemployment and regional inequality.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct reward for the factor of production known as capital?
A) Rent
B) Wages
C) Interest
D) Profit

A textile factory employs 40 workers, pays £12,000 per month in rent for its building, and uses £5,000 of raw cotton each month. In month 1, the factory's total revenue is £80,000 and its total costs are £65,000.

Calculate the factory's profit for month 1. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the correct method/formula: Profit = Total Revenue − Total Costs (£80,000 − £65,000); 1 mark for the correct answer of £15,000.

practice_questions.text: Explain why enterprise is considered a separate factor of production from labour.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the distinction (enterprise involves bearing risk / organising the other factors); 1 mark for developing this (labour receives a fixed wage regardless of outcome, whereas the entrepreneur only receives profit after all other costs are paid); 1 mark for a supporting example or further development (for example, a small business owner who invests savings into a start-up risks losing all that money if the business fails — unlike an employee who receives their wage either way).

practice_questions.text:
A car manufacturer decides to replace its human assembly line workers with industrial robots.

Using your knowledge of the factors of production, explain how this decision changes the combination of factors used in production.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the firm is substituting capital for labour; 1 mark for explaining what capital means in this context (man-made machinery used to produce other goods — here, industrial robots); 1 mark for explaining what happens to the labour factor (fewer workers are needed, reducing the wage bill); 1 mark for a further development or implication (for example, the firm may need to raise finance — incurring interest costs — to purchase the robots, and the entrepreneur bears the risk that the investment pays off through lower average costs and higher profit).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how low occupational mobility of labour can lead to unemployment and higher regional inequality in an economy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Develops a clear, connected chain of reasoning — e.g. when an industry such as steel or coal declines, workers with highly specific skills cannot easily transfer to growing sectors; this occupational immobility means they remain unemployed rather than filling vacancies in, for example, technology or services; wages in the declining region stagnate while wages in growing regions rise, widening regional inequality; the government may then need to spend more on welfare benefits, increasing public borrowing. Both the unemployment effect and the inequality effect are explained and linked.

Secure: Explains that low mobility causes unemployment and inequality with a clear reason for each, but the chain of reasoning is less developed or the link between them is not fully drawn.

Developing: Identifies that low mobility leads to unemployment or inequality but explanation is limited — for example, only stating that workers cannot move without explaining why this matters economically.

Emerging: A general point about labour mobility with little development or economic reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
'Enterprise is the most important factor of production in a market economy.'

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Without enterprise, the other three factors would not be combined — land, labour and capital are inert resources unless an entrepreneur identifies an opportunity, organises production and bears the financial risk.
- The prospect of profit motivates innovation: entrepreneurs launch new products and processes, driving productivity growth and raising living standards.
- Enterprise creates jobs: new firms generate demand for labour, increasing employment and wages across the economy.
- In a market economy, the price mechanism only works because profit-seeking entrepreneurs respond to price signals by allocating resources to where demand is greatest.

Arguments against:
- Without labour, enterprise is worthless: no workforce means no production, regardless of how good the business idea is.
- Capital is increasingly the binding constraint: in capital-intensive industries such as pharmaceuticals, energy or technology, the machinery, R&D infrastructure and intellectual property may matter more than the entrepreneur.
- Land underpins all production — natural resource availability constrains what can be produced regardless of entrepreneurial ambition.
- The relative importance of each factor varies by industry and time period: in agriculture, land dominates; in financial services, labour and enterprise dominate.

Judgement: The answer depends on the type and stage of development of the economy. In an early-stage market economy or a new industry, enterprise is arguably the catalyst that activates the others and is therefore most important. In a mature, capital-intensive industry, capital may be the binding constraint. The strongest answers will note that the factors are complementary — each is necessary — so calling any single one 'most important' is an oversimplification, though enterprise is uniquely responsible for combining the rest.

Mastering: Both sides developed with supported judgement that recognises the 'it depends on' logic, referencing type of industry or state of economy.
Secure: Both sides covered with a supported conclusion, but the judgement may lack nuance.
Developing: One side developed or both sides present but without a clear judgement.
Emerging: Simple points on one side only; limited or no economic reasoning.

knowledge_checks.q: Which factor of production earns rent as its reward?
In economics, what does the term 'capital' mean?
options: The money held in a bank account
The profit earned by a business
Man-made resources used to produce other goods and services
The wages paid to skilled workers

knowledge_checks.q: The person who combines the other factors of production and bears the risk of doing so is called an _____.
The ability of workers to move between different jobs or industries is called _____ mobility.
Match each factor of production to its reward:

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four factors of production?
flashcard_questions.a: The four factors are land (natural resources), labour (human effort), capital (man-made equipment), and enterprise (risk-bearing organisation).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the reward paid to the owners of land?
What is the reward paid for labour?
What is the reward paid to providers of capital?
What is the reward earned by an entrepreneur?
flashcard_questions.a: Profit — the income remaining after all other costs of production are paid.
Man-made resources used to produce other goods and services, such as machinery and vehicles.
Combines land, labour and capital, takes decisions about production, and bears the financial risk.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is land considered a scarce factor of production?
flashcard_questions.a: Its total supply is fixed — no new natural resources can be manufactured.

flashcard_questions.q: What is occupational mobility of labour?
flashcard_questions.a: The ability of workers to move between different jobs or industries.

flashcard_questions.q: What is geographical mobility of labour?
flashcard_questions.a: The ability of workers to move to a different location in order to find work.

flashcard_questions.q: Which factor of production is generally the least mobile, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Land — a natural resource such as a coal seam cannot be relocated.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the economic term for spending by firms on new machinery or buildings?
flashcard_questions.a: Investment — spending on capital goods to increase future productive capacity.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a capital good and one example of a consumer good.
flashcard_questions.a: Capital good: a factory robot. Consumer good: a smartphone bought by a member of the public.

glossary_terms.definition: The four types of resource used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and enterprise.
All natural resources used in production, including the physical land itself, minerals, oil, water, forests and fisheries.
The human effort, both physical and mental, used in the production of goods and services.
Man-made resources used to produce other goods and services, such as machinery, tools, vehicles, buildings and computers.
The human skill of combining the other factors of production and bearing the risk of doing so in order to produce goods or services.
A person who takes the risk of setting up and running a business, combining land, labour and capital in the hope of making a profit.
The ease with which a factor of production can be moved between different uses or different locations.
